about: Exposition is a Part IA coursework course in Michaelmas Term (8 timetabled sessions) that develops presentation, discussion and writing skills in groups led by a member of staff. Each student has their electronic filters lab report critically reviewed, gives a 10–15 minute talk on technical material and takes part in a debate or similar activity. It is not examined; it carries 26 coursework marks with a qualifying level of 18 (2026-27 credit notice).
topics: How to prepare and do well

notes.body:
Exposition is a Part IA coursework course in Michaelmas Term about communicating as an engineer: in writing, in a talk and in discussion. It has no lectures and no exam; the point is practice with feedback.

Why it exists
- The department's course page (last updated in 2018) starts from the idea that engineers get things done by persuading other people. Its example is persuading a board to back a project: that needs an accurate, readable discussion document (which may include technical material such as drawings) and then a face-to-face presentation in which you argue the case.
- The page also hopes the course will build confidence and the ability to take a lead.

How it runs
- The 2026-27 Part IA guide and coursework overview timetable Exposition as 8 sessions in Michaelmas, in groups led by a member of staff.
- Session locations and group leaders are listed on the Exposition Moodle site.
- Older details, possibly out of date: the course page (last updated in 2018) describes groups of twelve students meeting for two hours a week through the term, probably in a College rather than in the Department, with the audience being mainly your peers. Check the group size, timing and place for your year on Moodle.

What you do
According to the Part IA guide, each student:
- has their laboratory report on an electronic filters experiment critically reviewed in the group;
- gives a short talk, 10–15 minutes long, on technical material;
- takes part in a debate on a current technical topic, or another suitable activity, with topics chosen by the group leader.

The guide's intention is that the habits formed here carry through to later lab reports, project reports and presentations across the Tripos.

Note: the Exposition course page was last updated in 2018, so treat its practical details (group size, timing, location) as possibly out of date and check Moodle and your group leader for this year's arrangements.

Exposition is not examined in the written papers. It earns coursework credit.

Exposition credit
- In the 2026-27 Part IA coursework and examination credit notice, Exposition is worth 26 raw marks, with a qualifying level of 18.
- The notice does not break the 26 marks down by activity. Ask your group leader how the report review, the talk and the debate are judged, and what counts as satisfactory.
- Because marks are capped at the qualifying level, what matters in practice is reaching a satisfactory standard in every part and not missing sessions.

How Part IA coursework counts (2026-27 credit notice)
- All Part IA coursework is for standard credit. Once you reach the satisfactory standard, your marks for an activity are capped at its qualifying level, so there is no reward for going beyond it.
- The qualifying marks for all Part IA coursework add up to 200. The coursework mark that counts is your raw total minus 100, so it is at most 100.
- That is added to the four written papers, each marked out of 200, giving 900 marks in all for Part IA.
- You must complete every activity satisfactorily to get the full qualifying mark. Missing, late or unsatisfactory work leaves a shortfall, and the Part IA guide says shortfalls are deducted from your Tripos total.
- If illness or grave cause stops you completing coursework, the notice says you can apply to the EAMC for an allowance; for missed sessions, follow the department's rules on rearranging coursework and extensions.
- Submitted work must be your own, and any use of AI tools must follow University and departmental guidance.

notes.h: How to prepare and do well
notes.body:
Exposition rewards preparation and willingness to practise more than polish. The following is general good practice for each part; your group leader's instructions take priority.

The lab report review
- Your electronic filters report will be read critically by others, so write it for a reader who was not in the lab: say what you set out to find, how, what you found and what it means.
- Put the key result and conclusion early (a short summary), and make every figure stand on its own: numbered, captioned, axes labelled with quantities and units, and referred to in the text.
- Quote results to a sensible number of significant figures, compare them with theory, and discuss the sources of discrepancy rather than just listing them.
- When reviewing others' reports, be specific and constructive: point to the sentence or figure and suggest how to fix it.

The 10–15 minute talk
- Choose technical material you understand well enough to explain simply, and decide the one message the audience should take away.
- Structure it clearly: why it matters, the key idea, an example, and a conclusion that restates the message. Tell the audience where you are going.
- Keep slides sparse: one idea per slide, large readable figures, few words. Talk to the audience, not to the screen.
- Rehearse aloud with a timer. Running over is the commonest problem; cut material rather than speaking faster.
- Prepare for questions by thinking about what a sceptical listener would ask.

The debate
- Research both sides, because you need to anticipate the counter-arguments as well as make your own.
- Base claims on evidence you can name, separate facts from judgements, and keep points short.
- Listen to the other side and respond to what they actually said.

General
- Turn up to every session on time: attendance and satisfactory completion are what secure the credit.
- Use the feedback: the same skills are assessed again in later lab reports and project presentations, including the Structural Design Project report and presentation.

questions.q: Under the 2026-27 Part IA credit notice, how many marks does Part IA coursework contribute to the overall Tripos total?
options: It does not count, as long as it is satisfactory
questions.why: Qualifying coursework marks add up to 200, and the counted mark is the raw total minus 100, so at most 100; with four papers of 200 each the total is 900. 200 is the raw qualifying total, not the counted mark; 26 is the Exposition raw mark alone; and coursework does count, since shortfalls are deducted.
